title: 1MW No. 323 Always Say Less
author: Greg McKeown
summary: In this issue of 1-Minute Wednesday, Greg McKeown argues that every time we speak we are training others in how closely to listen to us next time. He builds on Robert Greene's advice to 'always say less than necessary,' presenting restraint as a signal of self-control that makes a person's words carry more weight. He pairs this with Steven Bartlett's idea of a 'contribution score,' illustrated by two colleagues: one whose constant half-formed thoughts led people to cut him off, and another whose rare contributions made the room lean in. McKeown's move is to reframe over-talking as a hidden cost to future influence rather than a harmless habit, noting that people who prove their value by contributing more may be teaching others to tune them out. He ties the principle back to Essentialism's 'fewer, but better' and closes with a practical filter: before speaking, ask whether the comment will help the group see what matters more clearly.
points: McKeown frames speech as reputation-building: each contribution teaches listeners how much attention your next one deserves.
Bartlett's 'contribution score' works like a credit score, a track record that precedes you and determines whether the room leans in or cuts you off.
Excessive talking carries a double cost, consuming time now and reducing the attention future, more essential words will receive.
A well-aimed question that surfaces the real problem is presented as worth more than a stream of proposed solutions.
The practical test before speaking is whether the comment will help the group see what matters more clearly; if not, keep listening.
quotes: Every time you speak, you teach people how closely to listen next time.
Restraint signals self-control. The person who can listen without rushing to speak commands more attention when they do. Their words carry weight because they have been selective with them.
When we can't stop talking, people may wonder what else we can't control. And the longer we talk, the more opportunities we create to say something we wish we hadn’t.
Like a credit score, your contribution score is a history that precedes you. People decide how much attention to give you based on what you have done with it before.

This is an uncomfortable idea for those of us accustomed to proving our value by contributing more. It is difficult to accept that we may be training people to pay us less attention—including when we finally have something essential to say.
The cost of unnecessary words isn't just the time they consume. It's the attention our future words no longer receive.
A question that reveals the real problem contributes more than ten proposed solutions.
